step1_summary: Chief complaint: 3-day history of frequent loose/watery diarrhoea

Symptoms:
  • Frequency: ~6–7 bowel motions/day
  • Character: loose, watery, no visible blood
  • Abdominal pain: cramp-like, intermittent, left lower abdomen
  • Associated: initial vomiting (now resolved), subjective fever at onset, weakness/shakiness, loss of appetite; tolerating fluids
  • Onset: abrupt, began 3 days ago after eating takeaway (Chinese restaurant 4 days ago)
  • No melena, no persistent vomiting, no night sweats
Medications/allergies: inhaler only; no other drugs mentioned; no allergies reported
Family/social history: married with 2 children (one child vomited once, no diarrhoea); non-smoker; does not drink alcohol; accountant; no travel mentioned
Vital signs / physical exam: none provided (telephone consult)

V: Ischaemic colitis: Sudden left-sided abdominal pain with diarrhoea can occur, especially if bloody; no bleeding documented but worth considering.
I: Viral gastroenteritis (e.g., norovirus): Acute onset watery diarrhoea, vomiting, low-grade fever, often self-limiting; family member also vomited.
Bacterial food-borne infection (e.g., Salmonella, Campylobacter, enterotoxigenic E. coli): Onset 1–3 days after takeaway meal; watery stools, abdominal cramps, feverish feeling.
Pre-formed toxin food poisoning (Staph aureus, Bacillus cereus): Could explain vomiting/diarrhoea soon after takeaway, though usually shorter course (<24 h).
N: Colorectal cancer: Can present with change in bowel habit and abdominal discomfort, but usually chronic and/or with bleeding.
D: Lactose intolerance or other malabsorption: Watery diarrhoea after dietary trigger; abdominal cramps.
I2: Drug-induced diarrhoea (e.g., antibiotics, metformin): Unlikely—no such medications reported.
C: Cystic fibrosis–related pancreatic insufficiency: Unlikely in adult without prior hx but could cause malabsorptive diarrhoea.
A: Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn’s): Can cause diarrhoea and abdominal pain; typically chronic, may have blood.
T: Abdominal trauma with bowel injury: No trauma history.
E: Hyperthyroidism: Can cause diarrhoea, weight loss, tremor, but onset usually gradual.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic triad of abrupt watery diarrhoea, vomiting and low-grade fever over a few days; often self-resolves; mild household transmission fits viral pattern.
supporting_evidence: No blood in stool or vomit
opposing_evidence: Localized left-sided abdominal pain (viral illness usually causes diffuse cramps)
History of takeaway meal raises bacterial possibility
